clinicalPearls: The classic tetrad comprises finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia
It localises to the dominant (usually left) inferior parietal lobule, particularly the angular gyrus
Finger agnosia is the inability to name or identify individual fingers on command despite intact sensation
Acalculia refers to acquired difficulty with calculation, and agraphia to impaired writing not explained by motor weakness
The full tetrad in isolation is uncommon; incomplete forms and associated aphasia or alexia are more typical
Common causes include dominant parietal infarction, tumour, and neurodegenerative disease
A developmental form is described in children with learning difficulties affecting the same domains
reference.pathophysiology: Gerstmann syndrome arises from damage to the dominant inferior parietal lobule, especially the angular gyrus and adjacent white matter, a region that integrates the body schema, spatial relationships, language, and numerical processing. Disruption here produces the characteristic combination of finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia. In adults the usual causes are ischaemic infarction in the middle cerebral artery territory, tumour, or a degenerative process, whereas a developmental variant reflects atypical maturation of the same cortical network.
additionalDifferentials: Broader aphasic syndromes from dominant parietal or temporal lesions
Confusional state or delirium impairing performance
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain focused on the dominant parietal lobe
Formal neuropsychological assessment of the four component deficits
Vascular imaging and stroke workup where infarction is suspected
Cognitive screening for coexisting language and praxis deficits
Evaluation for neurodegenerative disease when onset is insidious
Assessment for coexisting alexia and aphasia
redFlags: Acute onset suggesting a dominant parietal stroke requiring urgent assessment
Progressive cognitive decline suggesting a neurodegenerative or neoplastic cause
Associated headache or focal signs suggesting a mass lesion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; deficits from stroke may partially recover with rehabilitation, whereas those from progressive disease tend to worsen, and the developmental form persists but can be supported educationally.
pitfalls: Expecting the complete tetrad, when partial and mixed presentations are far more common
Attributing the deficits to global confusion rather than a focal parietal lesion
Missing coexisting aphasia or alexia that alters interpretation
Failing to image the dominant hemisphere when the tetrad is recognised
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause, whether acute stroke management and secondary prevention, tumour resection and oncological therapy, or care of neurodegenerative disease
Provide neurorehabilitation with occupational therapy and cognitive rehabilitation targeting finger agnosia, agraphia, acalculia, and right-left disorientation
Introduce compensatory strategies and assistive aids for writing and calculation difficulties
Offer educational support and accommodations for the developmental form in children
Use serial neuropsychological assessment to guide rehabilitation and track recovery or progression
Coordinate care across neurology, neuropsychology, and rehabilitation services
